text: Not to know anything, etc.  Greek art, poetry, and philosophy, Roman law, politics and conquest, trade and commerce and the grand and beautiful scenery of the lands where he labored are unmentioned in Paul's writings and discourses.  Only once at Athens did he quote an obscure Greek poet, whom he did not name.  See notes on  Acts 17:28 .

title: I Corinthians 2:3
text: Weakness. Physical weakness in part.  See  I Corinthians 11:30 Galatians 4:13 Galatians 4:14 .  In fear and in much trembling, not for consequences to himself but to his message, the truth of the gospel ( I Thessalonians 2:4 Titus 1:3 ; like the anxiety of a general for his army and his cause.

title: I Corinthians 2:4
text:
,5
 
Power. The power that changes hearts and lives ( I Corinthians 6:11 ).
 

 
Should not stand in the wisdom of men. Not in dependence on a human teacher, but on the divine power.

title: I Corinthians 2:6
text: Wisdom among them that are full grown. Many truths of the gospel can be appreciated only by those of some spiritual authority ( I Corinthians 4:1-2 Hebrews 5:12-14 I Peter 2:2 ).

title: I Corinthians 2:7
text: Mystery. In the Scriptures denoting; (a) something above the ordinary human understanding ( Mark 4:11 ); (b) something formerly hidden in the counsels of God, but afterwards revealed, as a plan understood by its own fulfillment.  Mystery ever accompanies vastness, depth, and power.

title: I Corinthians 2:9
text: Things which eye saw not, etc.  A free quotation from  Isaiah 64:4 .  This refers to spiritual truths and blessings not to be known through the senses or imagination, but only when divinely revealed.

title: I Corinthians 2:10
text:
,11
 
Through the Spirit. The meaning is that man's spirit is conscious of his human thoughts, feelings, and purposes; so the divine Spirit, of the divine thoughts, feelings and purposes.  The Spirit of God alone can reveal them.   I Corinthians 2:13-16  are a practical unfolding of this thought.

title: I Corinthians 2:14
text: The natural man, etc.  The unspiritual man cannot apprehend spiritual truth.

title: I Corinthians 3:1
text: Carnal. Not in the modern meaning of 'sensual,' but merely earthly, secular, worldly; having the worldly spirit of partisan strife, like politicians rather than Christian disciples.

title: I Corinthians 3:10
text:
Another buildeth thereon. Apollos, or any other successor.
 

 
Buildeth. Applied here not to the building, by each disciple, of his own Christian character, but to the building by the Christian teachers of character in others or in the church as a whole.

title: I Corinthians 3:13
text:
The day. Of judgment; the day of days.
 

 
The fire. A figurative expression for the severity of the test.  See  Matthew 7:24-27 .

title: I Corinthians 3:15
text: He himself shall be saved. The teacher who has built, however imperfectly, on the true foundation, himself shall be saved.  The apostle does not intend any bitter denunciation of sincerely erring teachers.

title: I Corinthians 3:16
text:
,17
 
Know ye not that ye are a temple of God, etc.  The meaning of the verses is not the same as that of  I Corinthians 6:19 I Corinthians 6:20 .  In  I Corinthians 3:16 I Corinthians 3:17  the reference is not to the body of the individual Christian as the temple, but to the whole company of believers collectively, the church, as forming a divine temple ( Ephesians 2:21 ).  Divisions and contentions tend to destroy the church; hence the warning here.

title: I Corinthians 3:18
text:
:21
 
If any man thinketh that he is wise, etc.  The apostle's advice is: Be spiritually simple-minded, and so wise to follow Christ alone.  Then all helpful spiritual leadership and all things else are yours in him.  Human and divine wisdom are distinguished here, as in  I Corinthians 1:25-30 I Corinthians 2:5-14 , but with new applications.

title: I Corinthians 4:1
text: Mysteries. See note on  I Corinthians 2:7 .

title: I Corinthians 4:5
text: His praise from God. Such praise as belongs to him in God's perfect judgment.

title: I Corinthians 4:6
text: The things which are written. No special text, but the teaching of the Scriptures as a whole, which no leader, however gifted, may supersede.

title: I Corinthians 4:7
text: Who maketh thee to differ? 'Thee' is general in meaning, equivalent to 'any one,' especially any one of the opposing teachers.  The English 'you' is often so used: 'you will find,' that is, any one will find.  In this and the following verses, Paul addresses the opposing teachers, first in the singular, then in the plural number, as if addressing them personally.  'Any superiority which any of you has is but the gift of God, not a cause of pride or partisanship.'

title: I Corinthians 4:8
text:
:13
 
Already are ye filled, etc.  Contrasting the prosperity which these leaders enjoyed, in a church already established and strong, with the hardships which Paul endured in founding it, and which he, in common with the other apostles, in new fields still endured.
 

 
Naked. Insufficiently clothed ( Matthew 25:36 James 2:15 ).
 

 
Working with our own hands. As he had done in Corinth ( Acts 18:3 Acts 20:23 ).

title: I Corinthians 4:15
text:
:20
 
Fathers. Paul claims authority as founder and 'father' of the church at Corinth.
 

 
Not in word, but in power. Not in eloquent speech, but in the leavening influence of the Spirit ( I Corinthians 2:4 I Corinthians 2:5 ).  This is the key to all.  Through everything and against everything the spiritual purity and power of the church and of the Christian life must be maintained.  This opens the way to the strictness of the next chapter.

title: I Corinthians 5:1
text:
Fornication. Denounced here as especially fatal to spiritual life in the church at Corinth, a city with a very dissolute population.  The discussion of the right relation of the sexes extends through  I Corinthians 5:1-7:40 , with a brief digression at  I Corinthians 6:1-9 .
 

 
His father's wife. His stepmother.  Whether the father was dead or divorced, and whether the new connection was in the form of marriage or concubinage, is not certain.  These considerations the apostle passed over as immaterial compared with the one fact that the woman was 'his father's wife.'  That was enough.

title: I Corinthians 5:2
text: Ye are puffed up. 'You are actually proud of such transgression.'  The views and practices here condemned by the apostle evidently had the approval of the false teachers, and were undoubtedly based upon a perverted view of Christian liberty-that faith sets the Christian free from obligation to obey the moral law.  Paul's opposition to such teachers was a contest for the very existence of the church as a spiritual body.

title: I Corinthians 5:4
text: Ye being gathered together. The separation was to be by the whole assembled church, punishment inflicted by the many ( II Corinthians 2:6 ).

title: I Corinthians 5:5
text: To deliver such a one unto Satan. The church was a body of those redeemed from the power of Satan; formal separation from their company was regarded as a delivery back to Satan, and to the world which is under his power, as the offender had chosen his service.  The sensual vices here condemned do naturally and commonly result in the destruction of the flesh.  That there was no sentence to perdition, or loss of the soul, is expressly stated in the concluding words, 'that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.'  See also  II Corinthians 2:6-10 , with which this verse must be compared in order to be understood.

title: I Corinthians 5:6
text:
:8
 
Leaven. Tolerated corruption will extend in the church as the action of leaven extends in meal.  The purification of the church by removal of the offenders is compared to the removal of leaven from Jewish homes at the feast of the Passover ( Exodus 12:15 Exodus 12:19 Exodus 13:3 Exodus 13:7 ).

title: I Corinthians 5:9
text:
In my epistle. Evidently referring to a previous letter.
 

 
To have no company, etc.   I Corinthians 5:9-13  explains the purpose of church discipline, the necessary separation of the obviously impure from a society that stands for purity, unless it would imperil its own existence.
 

 
Not at all, meaning, etc.  The apostle explains that his purpose is not the seclusion or separation of the disciples from the evil elements of the world in the common relations of life.  He does not mean that Christians should go out of the world.  See  John 17:15 .  Monastic seclusion is not for a moment contemplated.
 

 
No, not to eat. Have no familiar interaction.  In the case of one that is 'named a brother,' but is false to his profession, withdraw from all association indicating brotherhood.

title: I Corinthians 5:13
text: Put away. . from among yourselves. The limit of church action, carrying none of the meaning that in the later times came to be attached to the word 'excommunication.'

title: I Corinthians 6:1
text:
:8
 
Dare any of you, having a matter, etc.  Matters relating to the conduct of Christians are to be decided by Christians within the church ( I Corinthians 5:12-13 ).  Now the apostle applies the thought to controversies or claims of any kind.  These also are to be decided within the church.  The objection here is against Christians appearing voluntarily before the heathen courts of that day, with their recognition of heathen usages and divinities.  When summoned before them Paul himself did not deny their authority nor refuse to plead ( Acts 24:1-21 Acts 25:6-12 II Timothy 4:16 II Timothy 4:17 ).
 

 
Against his neighbor. That is, one Christian against another.

title: I Corinthians 6:4
text: If then ye have to judge, etc.  This is considered by many as a command rather than a question.  In either case the implication is the same, that those least esteemed in the church would be more appropriate judges of Christian matters than any heathen magistrates.

title: I Corinthians 6:5
text: To move you to shame. There is a touch of irony here; the plea is for Christian arbitration-in modern phrase, 'settlement out of court' in such cases.  The Hague Arbitral Court for national differences is here seen to emanate from Christian teaching.

title: I Corinthians 6:11
text: Ye were washed. Something far higher-a spiritual and divine cleansing from sin ( Hebrews 10:22 Revelation of John 7:14 ).

title: I Corinthians 6:12
text: All things are lawful, etc.  Paul here sets forth the doctrine of Christian liberty.  The Christian is not under the bondage of the ceremonial laws of Judaism.  He has freedom in the use of all the good things of God.  But this liberty must be modified at times by the exigencies of situations and surroundings.

title: I Corinthians 6:13
text:
Meats. Food in general.
 

 
The belly. The digestive tract, commonly expressed, in modern phrase, by 'the stomach.'
 

 
But the body is not, etc.  From this point the apostle returns to the subject of pure family and social relations through  I Corinthians 7:15-17 .

title: I Corinthians 6:18
text: Without the body. The body as mere material substance cannot do moral wrong.

title: I Corinthians 6:19
text: The temple of the Holy Spirit. ( II Corinthians 6:16 ).

title: I Corinthians 6:20
text: Price. The voluntary death of Christ ( I Peter 1:18 I Peter 1:19 ).

title: I Corinthians 7:1
text:
The things whereof ye wrote. The matters dealt with in this chapter, and others later, are treated in answer to written questions which the Corinthians had sent to the apostle.  The first question is concerning marriage and celibacy.  The frightful dissoluteness of the heathen society of the day led many earnest Christians to seek a remedy in the absolute separation of the sexes-a tendency which resulted in the vast number of hermits, monks, and nuns of a later period.
 

 
It is good for a man, etc.  It is well in view of the social conditions prevailing and the vicissitudes that were before the church at that period ( I Corinthians 7:25-27 ), a counsel of expediency, not a rule of duty.

title: I Corinthians 7:2
text: His own wife, etc.  Forbidding both concubinage and polygamy.

title: I Corinthians 7:7
text: As I myself. One of many passages that show the apostle Paul to have been unmarried ( I Corinthians 9:5 ).

title: I Corinthians 7:10
text: Not I, but the Lord. No longer his own opinion, as in  I Corinthians 7:6 , but the divine command of the perpetuity of marriage ( Matthew 5:32 Matthew 19:4-9 ).

title: I Corinthians 7:12
text: I, not the Lord. As to the special case of a Christian married to an unbelieving husband or wife the apostle had no special divine command, but only his own Christian interpretation of the divine law.

title: I Corinthians 7:14
text:
Is sanctified. Or brought into a hallowed relation.
 

 
Your children. They are in a like hallowed relation by their connection with the believer.

title: I Corinthians 7:21
text: A bondservant. Slavery, which was part of the Roman political system in the apostle's time, and is impossible to abolish, is given as a strong instance to inculcate the doing of Christian duty in an existing relation.

title: I Corinthians 7:22
text: Called in the Lord. Called into the Christian life.  'Called' has the same sense in  I Corinthians 7:17 I Corinthians 7:18 I Corinthians 7:20 .

title: I Corinthians 7:23
text: Bought with a price. See  I Corinthians 6:20 I Peter 1:18 I Peter 1:19 .

title: I Corinthians 7:25
text:
Virgins. Evidently, as  I Corinthians 7:36 I Corinthians 7:37  show, unmarried women still in their parents' home.  The Corinthians appear to have asked instruction on some cases of this kind.
 

 
I have no commandment of the Lord. No command laid down by Christ in his earthly ministry-nor any special revelation from him.

title: I Corinthians 7:26
text: The distress that is upon us. The unsettled conditions of the times and of the rising church, with the probability of persecution-all viewed as part of the 'tribulation.'

title: I Corinthians 7:28
text:
Hast not sinned. See  Ephesians 5:21 I Timothy 4:3 I Timothy 5:14 Hebrews 13:4 .
 

 
Tribulation in the flesh. The special cares and sorrows which those having families are subject to in troublous times.

title: I Corinthians 7:29
text:
:31
 
The time is shortened, etc.  The controlling thought is, all that is merely earthly is brief and transitory.

title: I Corinthians 7:31
text: The fashion of this world. This earthly scheme of things, with its buying and selling, its possessions, its joys and sorrows passeth away.

title: I Corinthians 7:36
text:
,37
 
If any man thinketh, etc.  To be understood in view of the then universal custom among Jews, Greeks, and Romans, that the father or guardian disposed of the daughter's hand.

title: I Corinthians 7:38
text: Shall do better. In view of the troublous times, as in  I Corinthians 7:26 .  The same thought is in view throughout this entire chapter.

title: I Corinthians 7:39
text:
,40
 
For so long time, etc.  Maintaining the widow's right of remarriage, with limitations as in  I Corinthians 7:26 I Corinthians 7:27 I Corinthians 7:38 .
 

 
Only in the Lord. In accordance with his Christian relations and duties.
 

 
I think that I also have, etc.  See  I Corinthians 7:6 I Corinthians 7:12 I Corinthians 7:25 .  Meant to be a mild form of asserting his assurance.

title: I Corinthians 8:1
text:
Things sacrificed to idols. In very many sacrifices, both among the Jews and the heathen, only a portion was consumed on the altar, the greater part being retained by the worshipper and carried away to be eaten by himself and friends or guests.  The eating of such sacrificial food was deemed an act of worship in honor of the divinity to whom it had been offered ( I Corinthians 10:18 I Corinthians 10:19 ).  In some cases the feast might be held within the Temple enclosure ( I Corinthians 8:10 ).  It might also be at the worshipper's home or elsewhere.  The sacrificial meat might even be 'sold in the shambles' ( I Corinthians 10:25 ).  For such sacrificial feasts among the Jews, see  Leviticus 7:15 Leviticus 7:16 Leviticus 22:30 I Samuel 16:2-5 .  The eating of such food by a Christian might easily seem, either to heathen or Christian observers, a recognition of idol worship  I Corinthians 8:10 .
 

 
Knowledge. Intellectual apprehension of truth and duty, which was held by many, especially among the philosophic Greeks, to be all that was required.  The apostle proceeds to show that there is something higher.
 

 
Knowledge puffeth up. Tends to self-confidence and arrogance.
 

 
Love edifieth. As in the margin, 'Buildeth up,' either the individual Christian or the church, as a whole, in Christian character and spiritual grace ( I Corinthians 14:4 I Corinthians 14:5 I Corinthians 14:12 Romans 14:19 Ephesians 4:12 I Thessalonians 5:11 ).

title: I Corinthians 8:2
text: If any man thinketh that he knoweth anything, etc. He who knows the most sees most clearly how much more there is to know.  In the field of knowledge humility sharpens vision.

title: I Corinthians 8:3
text:
If any man loveth God, etc.  Love brings the soul into touch with God who 'is love,' as no intellectual knowledge can do (1Jn 4.8).
 

 
 Is known by him.  In recognized and approved fellowship and communion ( Matthew 7:23 )

title: I Corinthians 8:4
text: That no idol is anything. Instructed Christians did not recognize idols as having any real existence, even as false divinities.  Idols were but empty names.

title: I Corinthians 8:7
text: There is not in all men that knowledge.  Many new converts had not attained this clear conception.  Love will care patiently and tenderly for such.

title: I Corinthians 8:9
text:
Take heed at last, etc. Love cares for the effect of one's example, especially upon those who have less knowledge, or are in any way spiritually 'weak.'
 

 
 A stumblingblock.  An occasion of yielding to temptation or sin.

title: I Corinthians 8:10
text:
Thee who hast knowledge.  An enlightened Christian must make allowance for the narrowness of one who has not his knowledge, and must sometimes therefore deny himself what he sees to be only innocent and beneficial.
 

 
 Sitting at meat in an idol's temple. The strongest case cited as an example.  The weak brother 'sees' the act, but cannot read the motive, which is known only to God.

title: I Corinthians 8:13
text: If meat causeth my brother to stumble, etc.  Rather than risk such a result as mentioned in  I Corinthians 8:11-12 , I will make any, even the uttermost, self-denial.  Compare this chapter with  I Corinthians 10:18-33 ; also with  Romans 14:1-23 , which discusses the eating of food forbidden by the Jewish ceremonial law, applying to that case the same principles.

title: I Corinthians 9:1
text: Have I not seen Jesus our Lord, etc.  Paul here discusses his apostolic authority and conduct, evidently in answer to objections brought by some of the opposing parties mentioned in  I Corinthians 7:11-12 I Corinthians 3:8-22 , and perhaps mentioned in the Corinthians' letter of inquiry, 'the things whereof ye wrote.' Those who called themselves 'of Cephas' and 'of Christ' apparently objected to Paul that he was not one of the original twelve, and had not attended the personal ministry of Jesus.

title: I Corinthians 9:2
text: The seal of mine apostleship. The fact that God had so blessed his labors as to lead the Corinthians to Christ proved Paul's call to be genuine.

title: I Corinthians 9:3
text:
Defence. Probably referring to what follows.
 

 
 Them that examine me. Those who sit in Judgment on me; the opposers already mentioned.

title: I Corinthians 9:4
text: To eat and to drink. That is, to receive food and drink at the cost of the church; a right given by Christ himself ( Matthew 10:9 Matthew 10:10 Luke 10:4-8 )

title: I Corinthians 9:5
text:
To lead about a wife. Not only to be married, but to be accompanied by one's wife in ministerial travels among the churches, both being supported by the church, as indicated by  I Corinthians 9:4 .
 

 
 The rest of the apostles, etc.  Plainly showing that these were married, notably Cephas or Peter (Mk 1.30, 31).

title: I Corinthians 9:6
text: Working. That is, for our own support, while preaching the gospel ( Acts 18:3 Acts 20:34 Acts 20:35 ).

title: I Corinthians 9:7
text:
:14
 
 What soldier ever serveth, etc.  These verses contain a defence of the right of ministerial support.  Paul feared lest his example should be pleaded against that right.
 

 
 Carnal things. Earthly enjoyments and supplies.

title: I Corinthians 9:16
text: Woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel.  Not a statement of the universal ministerial call, but of the condemnation which had stricken him down as a persecutor, and of the obligation which laid upon him at his conversion the necessity of preaching the gospel.

title: I Corinthians 9:18
text: My reward.  No earthly recompense, but the privilege of giving the gospel freely to men.

title: I Corinthians 9:20
text: Became as a Jew.  In all innocent compliances.

title: I Corinthians 9:21
text:
Them that are without law.  Those who are without the ceremonial law; the Gentiles.
 

 
 Not being without law to God.  Never disobeying the moral law, but pushing the ceremonial law aside in order to win those who have never been bound by it.

title: I Corinthians 9:22
text: Gain the weak. With all generous and self denying consideration of the needs of their weakness ( I Corinthians 8:9-13 ).

title: I Corinthians 9:23
text: That I may be a joint partaker thereof.  Win the gospel's glorious reward.

title: I Corinthians 9:25
text:
Exerciseth self-control in all things. The comparison is to the Isthmian games celebrated with great splendor at Corinth.  The athletes of that day, as of our own, denied themselves every indulgence that would hinder them from winning the prize.
 

 
 A corruptible crown.  A fading wreath.  The prize in the games was a wreath of laurel, wild olive, pine, or sometimes only of parsley.
 

 
 But we an incorruptible. ( I Timothy 4:8 I Peter 5:4 Revelation of John 2:10 Revelation of John 4:10 )

title: I Corinthians 9:26
text: As not beating the air.  The figure changes to that of the boxer.  Not like such a one 'beating the air' with empty flourishes while no antagonist is within reach.

title: I Corinthians 9:27
text:
I buffet my body.  I beat down all bodily appetites and desires.
 

 
 Bring it onto bondage.  Reduce the physical into entire subjection to the spiritual nature.
 

 
 After that I have preached to others. See  Matthew 7:22 Matthew 7:23 
 

 
 Rejected. Either as unworthy to be a preacher or unworthy of the crown of life.

title: I Corinthians 10:1
text: Our fathers.  Many of the Corinthians were not Israelites, but the apostle Paul, as a Jew, naturally refers to the sacred history of his own people.  The indication is that the Old Testament Scriptures were used in the Christian Church, and that even Gentile converts were expected to be familiar with them.

title: I Corinthians 10:2
text: Baptized unto Moses.  The allusion here is to baptism in the spiritual sense, since the Israelites were not wet by  the cloud or the sea ( Exodus 14:19 Exodus 14:22 ).  The passage of the Red Sea separated the Israelites from their slavery in Egypt, as baptism separated the believer from slavery to sin and the world.

title: I Corinthians 10:3
text:
, 4
 
 Spiritual food, etc.  So-called as affording spiritual nourishment- not mere manna ( Exodus 16:14-26 ) nor mere water ( Exodus 17:5 Exodus 17:6 ); but symbols of Jehovah's care.
 

 
 A spiritual rock that followed them.  There is no evidence nor probability that the apostle here refers to an obscure and late rabinnical tradition that the rock of  Exodus 17:5 Exodus 17:6  and of  Numbers 20:7-11 , followed, or that the streams followed, the Israelites in their journeys.  He uses the 'rock' as a symbol and type of the Angel of the Covenant that 'followed' the people, a 'spiritual rock,' and explains the statement by the words, 'that rock was Christ.'

title: I Corinthians 10:6
text: Examples. Not for imitation, but for warning.  See  I Corinthians 10:11 .

title: I Corinthians 10:11
text: The ends of the ages.  The last days, the closing dispensation, called also the 'last time' (1Jn 2.18).

title: I Corinthians 10:12
text: Him that thinketh he standeth.  Directed especially against the self-confidence of many of the Corinthians, but conveying a universal warning.

title: I Corinthians 10:14
text: Flee from idolatry.  The apostle here returns to the question of food offered to idols.  See  I Corinthians 8:1-13  and notes thereon.

title: I Corinthians 10:15
text:
, 17
 
 The cup of blessing, etc.  The spiritual feast of the Christian, the Lord's supper, signifies consecration to and unity with Christ ( I Corinthians 11:27-34 ).  The reality of the sacramental gifts and blessings is also here asserted.

title: I Corinthians 10:19
text: That an idol is anything.  A question to which a negative answer is expected, equivalent to an emphatic denial.

title: I Corinthians 10:20
text:
Sacrifice to demons.  The heathen divinities, impersonations of human passions, crimes, and vices raised to superhuman power, are fitly called demons.  Gentiles sacrificed to divinities such as these, though they had no real existence ( I Corinthians 8:4 I Corinthians 10:19 ).
 

 
 Communion with demons.  The idol feast symbolized communion with the idol (demon), just as the Lord's cup and table symbolized communion with Christ.

title: I Corinthians 10:21
text: Ye cannot drink the cup, etc.  See  Matthew 6:24 Luke 16:13 .

title: I Corinthians 10:23
text: All things are lawful, etc.  See  I Corinthians 6:12 .

title: I Corinthians 10:25
text:
:27
 
 Eat, asking no question.  The food to be partaken of is of no consequence except by the recognized significance of its associations.  If no such significance is known or recognized, no harm or wrong is done; no idol worship is then symbolized.
 

 
 For conscience sake.  The Christian is not to disturb business or social usages by obtruding conscientious scruples where no moral wrong is manifest.

title: I Corinthians 10:28
text: But if any man say unto you, etc. If others recognize the food as so dedicated that your partaking would seem to approve a wrongful dedication, then abstain.

title: I Corinthians 10:29
text:
,30
 
 Why is my liberty judged, etc. That is, why should I be obliged to use my liberty so as to come under condemnation before another's conscience?  The word here translated 'judged' often has the sense of condemnatory judgment ( Acts 7:7 Romans 3:7 Hebrews 13:4 ).
 

 
 That for which I give thanks.  That which is so innocent in my view that I can even give thanks for it- why should I indulge in it, if it will cause me and my religion to be evilly spoken of?

title: I Corinthians 11:1
text: In all things.  'All' is often used in the New Testament in a general sense, not necessarily including every one ( Matthew 3:5 Matthew 3:6 Matthew 21:10 Luke 21:38 ).  Here the apostle himself mentions some exceptions, but thoughtfully begins by commending their faithfulness on the whole or for the most part.

title: I Corinthians 11:2
text: Traditions. Matters orally delivered; ordinarily meaning handed down from generation to generation; but here referring to the precepts of doctrine or duty orally delivered by the apostles to the churches in the first Christian generation.

title: I Corinthians 11:3
text:
The head of every man is Christ.  There are two Greek words for 'man'; one for man as a human being; the other contrasting man with woman or child; the latter form is used for man in every instance in this chapter ( I Corinthians 3:16 ). Christ is normally and rightly the head of every man, actually of every Christian.
 

 
 The head of the woman is the man.  More fully explained in  Ephesians 5:22 Ephesians 5:23 
 

 
 The head of Christ is God.  Said of Christ in his mediatorial capacity ( I Corinthians 15:28 John 8:29 John 14:24 John 14:28 ).

title: I Corinthians 11:4
text:
:16
 
 Every man praying or prophesying, etc.  The propriety of covering or veiling the head is one to be understood in accordance with the customs of those countries at that period.  The veil in public places was then and there the mark of honorable and modest womanhood, and hence not to be disregarded by the Christian woman.  Other times and lands have other forms of expressing deference and modesty.  Any defiance of custom, which would indicate the lack of these qualities, would be censurable still.
 

 
 Every woman praying or prophesying. This, in connection with ( I Corinthians 11:4 ), seems to indicate a recognized right of woman to 'pray or prophesy' in the Christian assemblies in a decorous manner, and this was apparently a limitation upon the seemingly absolute prohibition of ( I Corinthians 14:34 I Corinthians 14:35 ).

title: I Corinthians 11:11
text: In the Lord.  The spiritual unity of man and wife, in spite of differences of social relations and requirements, is meant ( Galatians 3:28 ).

title: I Corinthians 11:18
text:
, 19
 
 Divisions.  See  I Corinthians 1:11 I Corinthians 1:12 I Corinthians 3:1 I Corinthians 3:4 .

title: I Corinthians 11:20
text:
:22
 
 When therefore ye assemble, etc.  Disorders at the Lord's supper may have arisen from connecting it with the 'love-feasts' of the early church.  See notes on  Acts 2:42 Acts 2:47 .
 

 
 Have ye not houses to eat and to drink in?  The fault was in making the sacrament a supper, a mere ordinary meal.  The rudeness and selfishness displayed were disgraceful incidents.

title: I Corinthians 11:23
text:
:25
 
 For I received of the Lord, etc.  This is the fourth account of the institution of the Lord's supper; the other three are in  Matthew 26:26-28 Mk 14.22-24; Lu 22.17-20.  The repetition in all four instances of the words of institution make them the most absolutely certain of all the utterances of our Lord.

title: I Corinthians 11:27
text: Guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.  'Of' has here the sense of 'in respect to'; guilty of profaning the elements used in the communion of which the Lord had said: 'This is my body; this is my blood.'

title: I Corinthians 11:30
text: Many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep.  Numerous commentators regard the illness as physical, and the sleep as the sleep of death; both sent as divine judgment.  Others hold that spiritual weakness and sickness and apathy or deadness (sleep) of soul are indicated.

title: I Corinthians 12:1
text: Concerning spiritual gifts.  that is, the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit here and elsewhere referred to, the existence of which is not declared as a thing to be proved, undisputed fact ( Acts 2:1-5 Acts 16:16-18 Acts 19:1-7 ).   I Corinthians 12:12-14  are a continuous discussion of spiritual gifts.   I Corinthians 13:1-13 , which seems an episode, is part of the discussion, only rising to a higher key in showing the supremacy of love.

title: I Corinthians 12:2
text:
Ye were Gentiles.  Evidently the greater part of the church; therefore needing the simplest and most elementary instruction.
 

 
 Dumb idols.  See  I Corinthians 8:4 I Corinthians 10:19 .

title: I Corinthians 12:3
text:
No man speaking, etc. The supreme test of seemingly prophetic utterance - The sincere acknowledgment of the lordship of Jesus.
 

 
 Saith. Jesus is anathema.  Not necessarily in those words, but what amounts to the same; denying him as Lord and Redeemer.  'Anathema' signifies 'an accursed thing,'
 
'an abomination.' By some authorities the phrase 'says Jesus is anathema' is taken to mean 'reviles him as an impostor, justly put to death.'  There appear to have been some Jews who still denied the Messiahship of Christ; or Greeks, inflated with the philosophical 'wisdom,'  I Corinthians 1:18-22 , who desired to share the spiritual freedom and privileges of the Christian church and supposed themselves or pretended to be under divine inspiration while denying Christ.  That denial proved them false.
 

 
 Say, Jesus is Lord. Of course with honest utterance and purpose.
 

 
 But in the Holy Spirit. To such conviction one must be divinely led ( Matthew 11:25-27 Matthew 16:16 Matthew 16:17 ).

title: I Corinthians 12:4
text: Diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.  Gifts differing according to the purpose and choice of God, but altogether making up a divine harmony ( I Corinthians 12:11 ).

title: I Corinthians 12:7
text: To profit withal. Literally, for advantage or utility, that is, to the church, not for pride or display.

title: I Corinthians 12:8
text: Wisdom. In this verse 'wisdom' may refer to practical duties, and 'knowledge' to the doctrinal part of the Christian system, perhaps the mysteries of  I Corinthians 13:2 .

title: I Corinthians 12:9
text:
Faith. Most probably a faith remarkable in its degree, strong enough to overcome great obstacles, as compared with the simple but untried and undeveloped faith of the inexperienced believers.
 

 
 Gifts of healings. See  Acts 3:6-8 Acts 9:32-41 Acts 19:11 Acts 19:12 .

title: I Corinthians 12:10
text:
Workings of miracles. Miraculous powers in general, beyond the healing of the sick.
 

 
 Prophecy.  The utterance of truth under divine inspiration.  The foretelling of future events might be included ( Acts 20:23 Acts 21:10 Acts 21:11 ), but only as a small and incidental part of the prophetic gift.  In  I Corinthians 12:28  prophecy is placed second in rank among the spiritual gifts; it is also prominently mentioned in  I Corinthians 14:1-5 .
 

 
 Discernings of spirits. Power to perceive whether a profession or utterance was truly or falsely made.
 

 
 Kinds of tongues. Emotional ecstatic utterances.  See  I Corinthians 14:2  and note thereon.
 

 
 Interpretation of tongues. By one able to make intelligible the utterance which neither the speaker nor his audience could clearly understand.  For the importance of this see  I Corinthians 14:13 I Corinthians 14:27 I Corinthians 14:28 .

title: I Corinthians 12:12
text: The body. The church, with its many members and their various gifts, is likened to the human body, as explained in  I Corinthians 12:27 .  See  Ephesians 1:22 Ephesians 1:23 Ephesians 4:15 Ephesians 4:16 Colossians 1:18

title: I Corinthians 12:28
text: First apostles, etc. An enumeration which begins with persons- apostles, prophets, teachers, but then passes over to the gifts exercised, showing that the main thought is of the gifts, which are mentioned in the order of their importance.  We need not supposed the enumeration to be mathematically precise.  The apostleship is first, as the apostles were the leaders and founders of the church; prophecy is second, for its spiritual helpfulness, as urged in  I Corinthians 14:1-40 : teaching next, as giving the sure basis of accepted truth; miracles and gifts of healing follow, but in order reversed from 1 Co 12.9, 10; helps, probably the work of caring for the sick and needy ( Acts 6:1 Acts 6:3 ), but not necessarily limited to the official deacons; governments, or offices of church administration; last of all, the divers ''kinds of tongues,'' which the Corinthians seem to have prized so highly.

title: I Corinthians 12:31
text: A most excellent way. A way by which to obtain and use the highest gifts.

title: I Corinthians 13:1
text:
If I speak, etc. In this chapter the thought rises above all special manifestations of spiritual power to the pure unselfish and perfect devotion of the soul to God, the essence of whose being is love ( I John 4:8 ).  All else is inferior to this single grace.
 

 
 The tongues of men. Of all men, of every nation.
 

 
 And of angels. There is here no declaration regarding any speech of angels, but simply a comparison carried to its highest imaginative point, even to the language which angels may be supposed to speak.
 

 
 And have not love. Love in its highest reach - a pure and full affection and devotion towards God and man. See  Matthew 5:44 Matthew 22:37-39 John 3:16 John 13:1 John 13:34 John 14:15 John 14:31 John 15:9 John 15:12 John 17:23-26 I Corinthians 2:9 I Corinthians 8:3 Ephesians 5:2 I Peter 1:8 I John 3:11 I John 3:14 I John 4:8 I John 4:11 I John 4:12 ).
 

 
 Sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. Mere empty sound.

title: I Corinthians 13:2
text:
Prophecy. See  I Corinthians 12:10  and note thereon.
 

 
 Knowledge. See  I Corinthians 12:8  and note thereon.
 

 
 Faith. See  I Corinthians 12:9  and note thereon.

title: I Corinthians 13:3
text:
Bestow. The meaning of the original word is to feed by bits or morsels, indicating the giving of all of one's means in charity to needy persons.  But even such giving might be without love ( Matthew 6:1 Matthew 6:2 ).
 

 
 Give my body to be burned. When martyrdom came to be esteemed glorious, there were instances of persons who met it in an unchristian spirit, as is recorded of one who on his way to the stake refused to forgive one who implored his pardon.

title: I Corinthians 13:4
text:
Suffereth long. With meek and undiscouraged patience under wrongs, like that of the suffering Christ.
 

 
 Is kind. Tenderly thoughtful and generous in word and act.
 

 
 Envieth not. Is not disturbed by any superiority of others.
 

 
 Vaunteth not itself. It is not boastful.
 

 
 Is not puffed up. Is not vain, proud, arrogant, or haughty.

title: I Corinthians 13:5
text:
Doth not behave itself unseemly. Avoids, for the sake of others, all conduct that may seem unworthy or may be a cause of reproach, such as 'the sitting at meat' in an idol's temple.  See  I Corinthians 8:10  and notes thereon.
 

 
 Seeketh not its own. Is unselfish.
 

 
 Is not provoked. Does not readily find causes of provocation; is not irritable.
 

 
 Taketh not account of evil. Does not put it on record, as in an account book, for remembrance or revenge.

title: I Corinthians 13:6
text:
Rejoiceth not in unrighteousness. Has no pleasure in prosperity or success unrighteously obtained; or, as some interpret, in hearing or telling of unrighteousness in others.
 

 
 Truth. Of doctrine, utterance, and action.

title: I Corinthians 13:7
text: All things. That is, all that may be rightly borne, believed, hoped, or endured.  See  I Corinthians 11:2  and note thereon.

title: I Corinthians 13:8
text:
:10
 
 Love never faileth. Love is immortal as part of the heavenly life, where tongues, prophecies and human knowledge shall be superseded.

title: I Corinthians 13:11
text: Childish things. The toys, the plays, and the lessons of childhood.  Like these will the highest earthly attainments seem hereafter.

title: I Corinthians 13:12
text: In a mirror. The easily tarnished metallic mirror of ancient times.

title: I Corinthians 13:13
text: Now abideth faith, hope, love.  They are all eternal: faith, in the forever unsearchable wisdom of God: hope, in the forever increasing glory and blessedness of heaven: love, the chief of the three, as part of the divine nature.

title: I Corinthians 14:1
text: Prophesy. 'Prophesy' in the Scriptures signifies not merely nor chiefly foretelling the future, but uttering truth under divine inspiration.  Large portions of the books of the Old Testament prophets, as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, etc., are devoted to the description of present or past events, advice, reproof, and the like.  This sense of the word prophesy is especially prominent in the New Testament ( I Corinthians 14:24 I Corinthians 14:25 I Corinthians 12:10  and note thereon).

title: I Corinthians 14:2
text: He that speaketh in a tongue, etc. Speaking in a tongue or tongues, a kind of ecstatic utterance, is in 1 and 2 Corinthians different from speaking with 'other tongues,' that is, in foreign languages, as recorded in  Acts 2:4 .  The utterance of him who spoke in a tongue might be unknown to all the hearers.  See  I Corinthians 14:11 .  In  Acts 2:3-13  the speaking with tongues apparently means speaking in foreign languages; but in 1 and 2 Corinthians the gift is best taken to signify an ecstatic utterance, not intelligible until interpreted.  See  I Corinthians 14:19 .

title: I Corinthians 14:4
text: Edifieth himself. He himself is supposed to understand the words he speaks.

title: I Corinthians 14:6
text: If I come unto you, speaking with tongues. See  I Corinthians 14:18 .

title: I Corinthians 14:11
text: A barbarian. This had no reference to personal character or grade of civilization.  The Greeks called every one not a Greek a barbarian, that is, one who spoke an unintelligible tongue.

title: I Corinthians 14:12
text: The edifying of the church. The purpose that should be controlling.  See  I Corinthians 14:12 I Corinthians 14:26 I Corinthians 8:1 I Corinthians 10:23 Ro15.2; Eph 4.12, 16, 29.

title: I Corinthians 14:13
text: Pray that be may interpret. The two powers of speaking in a tongue and of interpreting the utterance seem not to have been always joined in the same person.

title: I Corinthians 14:18
text: I speak with tongues more than you all. The only definite statement that Paul possessed the gift of tongues, which he mentions here incidentally.  His use of Greek to the chief captain ( Acts 21:37 ) and of the Aramaic or 'Hebrew' ( Acts 22:2 ) implies nothing miraculous or more than any well educated Jew of that day might have done.

title: I Corinthians 14:23
text:
Men unlearned or unbelieving.  The meetings were public; unbelievers could freely come.  The Christian assemblies were never secret until persecution made them so.
 

 
 Say that ye are mad.  Such visitors being evidently unable to understand the utterances.

title: I Corinthians 14:24
text: He is reproved, etc. By the power of spiritual truth spoken in a language with which he is familiar.  See  John 16:8 .

title: I Corinthians 14:25
text: Fall down on his face.  With the face near the ground or the floor, the forehead supported on clasped hands; the oriental posture of adoration and supplication.  See  Matthew 17:6 Matthew 26:39 Revelation of John 7:11 .

title: I Corinthians 14:26
text: Each one hath, etc. Abundant resources and readiness; although these might tend to confusion unless discretely ordered.  There was one rule for this: Let all things be done unto edifying.

title: I Corinthians 14:27
text:
By two, or at the most three. Paul considered the gift of speaking in a tongue a dangerous one, to be guardedly manifested.
 

 
 In turn. One at a time, indicating that two or more may have been previously allowed to speak at once, producing the 'confusion' of  I Corinthians 14:33 .
 

 
 And let one interpret. 'That the church may receive edifying' ( I Corinthians 14:5 ).

title: I Corinthians 14:29
text: Let the prophets speak by two or three. Two or three such exercises on one occasion, following each other in orderly sequence.

title: I Corinthians 14:30
text: But if a revelation be made, etc. Let any speaker close his remarks if he perceives that another has received a sudden revelation.

title: I Corinthians 14:31
text: One by one. One at a time; two or three of one kind of exercise to be heard in immediate sequence.

title: I Corinthians 14:32
text: The spirits of the prophets are subject, etc. Those who exercise the prophetic gift must control it.

title: I Corinthians 14:33
text:
Confusion. The apostle meant: be sure God cannot work in you in confusion, for that is not His way, and does not fittingly manifest nor can it glorify Him.
 

 
 Peace. Goes fitly with the 'love' of  I Corinthians 13:1-13 .  The two terms are often joined.  See  I Corinthians 7:15 John 14:27 John 16:33 Acts 10:36 II Corinthians 13:11 Galatians 5:22 .

title: I Corinthians 14:34
text:
, 35
 
 Let the women keep silence, etc. To be read in connection with  I Corinthians 11:5 I Corinthians 11:13 .  In those verses praying or prophesying by women under proper conditions seems to be permitted.  The force of the present passage has been much disputed, some expositors and churches holding that the prohibition is for all places and all times; others urging that it was local and temporary, for the places and the period with reference to which the apostle wrote, where the general seclusion of women would cause any public activity to be held 'shameful,' like the dispensing with the veil.

title: I Corinthians 14:39
text: Let all things be done decently, etc. The object of all the special instructions here given.

title: I Corinthians 15:3
text:
First of all. Among the first and fundamental truths of the gospel.  See  I Corinthians 2:2 Acts 17:31 .
 

 
 That which I also received. From the other apostles ( Acts 9:27 Acts 9:28 Galatians 1:18 Galatians 1:19 ). Also, direct revelation at his own conversion.
 

 
 According to the Scriptures. In fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy.  See  Isaiah 53:1-12 Luke 24:44-46 .

title: I Corinthians 15:4
text:
:7
 
 That he was buried. An important fact, suggesting the reality of both the death and the resurrection.
 

 
 Raised on the third day. The narrative of the resurrection by the Evangelists relates what had long been orally taught, so that Paul had 'received' it ( I Corinthians 15:3 )  Verses  I Corinthians 15:4-7  contain the first written story of the resurrection of Christ.  It was written about twenty-five years after the event, that is about 55-56 A.D. The list of witnesses here given is not complete.
 

 
 Cephas. (Peter). See  John 21:11-21 .
 

 
 James. Probably the Lord's brother.  See  Acts 15:13 Galatians 1:19 .  The appearance to James is not recorded in the gospels, but Peter and James were both personally known to Paul.
 

 
 Above five hundred brethren at once. Perhaps on the mountain in Galilee.  See  Matthew 28:16 Matthew 28:17 .
 

 
 The greater part remain. They were still living when Paul wrote this epistle and might be met from time to time, or sought out and talked with as witnesses.
 

 
 The twelve. ( I Corinthians 15:5 ).
 

 
 All the apostles. ( I Corinthians 15:7 )  Evidently two appearances.  See  Matthew 28:16 Matthew 28:17 Luke 24:33-36 John 20:26-29 Acts 1:2 Acts 1:6-11 .

title: I Corinthians 15:8
text:
To me also. On the road to Damascus, at his conversion. (  .)
 

 
 The child untimely born.  Born out of the ordinary course of nature, since Paul did not become an apostle, as the others did, by personal attendance on the earthly ministry of Jesus and by personally witnessing the scenes of the resurrection.

title: I Corinthians 15:9
text:
The least of the apostles. As the child untimely born is small and weak; an expression of deep humility.
 

 
 Because I persecuted. The offence which he could never forgive himself.  See  I Timothy 1:13 .

title: I Corinthians 15:11
text: I or they. By the appearance of Christ to him at his conversion, Paul could be counted with the other apostles  as a personal witness of the resurrection.  See  I Corinthians 9:1 Acts 22:14 Acts 22:18 .

title: I Corinthians 15:12
text: That there is no resurrection of the dead. Some of the Corinthians affirmed that resurrection of the dead is, on general principles, impossible.  Those who took this ground were doubtless the advocates of the so-called philosophic 'wisdom' elsewhere mentioned.  See  I Corinthians 1:18-25 I Corinthians 2:6-8 I Corinthians 3:19 .

title: I Corinthians 15:13
text: But if there is no resurrection, etc. The general denial of the possibility of any resurrection of the dead would imply a denial of the fact of Christ's resurrection.

title: I Corinthians 15:14
text: Then is our preaching vain. A dead Christ cannot be our Redeemer. Throughout the Acts and the Epistles the inspiration is that of a risen and still living Christ.  See  Acts 2:24-32 Acts 5:30-32 Acts 10:38-43 Acts 13:28-37 .

title: I Corinthians 15:15
text: False witnesses of God. Every hypothesis as to imagination, hallucination, or ecstasy is here met and set aside.  The apostle maintains that the witnesses, of whom he was one, are competent, and if the events to which they testify did not occur, they are 'false witnesses.' He meets squarely and openly the issue which still remains to be met: Could men of such principles, who sacrificed and suffered what they did for their testimony, be 'false witnesses'?

title: I Corinthians 15:18
text: Then they also that are fallen asleep, etc. Those who have perished include all who have died a martyr's death for Christ's sake. 'Fallen asleep' is the familiar Christian figure of speech for death. See  I Corinthians 15:6 I Corinthians 15:20 I Corinthians 15:51 Matthew 27:52 Mark 5:39 John 11:11 Acts 7:60 I Thessalonians 4:14 .

title: I Corinthians 15:19
text: If we have only hoped in Christ in this life. Said in view of the sacrifices and sufferings of the Christians of that day for Christ's sake.  If their hope of eternal life was illfounded, such sacrifices and sufferings were indeed 'most pitiable.'  See  II Corinthians 11:23-27 .

title: I Corinthians 15:23
text: Christ the first-fruits. The pledge of the result, as the first sheaf is of the harvest.  See  Leviticus 23:10 Leviticus 23:11 Leviticus 23:20 .

title: I Corinthians 15:28
text: The Son also himself be subjected. See  John 14:28 John 17:4 John 17:5 .

title: I Corinthians 15:30
text: Why do we also stand in jeopardy, etc. Why, if there is nothing to hope for beyond the grave? 'We' may denote all the Christians of that day, or, preeminently, the apostles.

title: I Corinthians 15:31
text: I die daily. I live in daily exposure to death.

title: I Corinthians 15:32
text: Fought with beasts, etc. There is no record of any such encounter, and Paul's Roman citizenship would possibly have saved him from exposure to wild beasts in the arena.  The single Greek word translated 'fought with beasts' was figuratively used for any dangerous or dreadful conflict, and this use is here indicated by the phrase 'after the manner of men,' that is, speaking after the manner of men or using a common mode of speech.  Paul's experience with the mob at Ephesus ( Acts 19:23 Acts 19:24 ) might very naturally be figuratively described.  Nevertheless the literal interpretation may very easily be possible.

title: I Corinthians 15:35
text:
:44
 
 How are the dead raised?  Paul here considers a materialistic objection which has sprung up anew in every age.  How can the particles of this body, when once it has been disintegrated and scattered, be reassembled into the same living organism?  The apostle makes no attempt to show that they every will be, but argues for the preservation of essential identity by examples of the infinite variety of God's creative power.
 

 
 A bare grain. A naked kernel of wheat, from which there springs another body, not composed of the same particles, since all but the life germ has decayed in the ground; but the new body is far more glorious.  The seed so transformed  produces a body of its own, possessing not the same particles, but essential identity, wheat always producing wheat, etc.  Christ uses the same figure of speech in regard to his own death ( John 12:24 ).

title: I Corinthians 15:40
text: Celestial bodies and bodies terrestrial. Alluding to the vast differences in the nature and glory of earth, sun, moon and stars, yet all within the easy sweep of God's creative power.

title: I Corinthians 15:42
text: So also is the resurrection of the dead. The risen body differs vastly from the buried earthly body; it contrasts corruption with power.

title: I Corinthians 15:45
text: The last Adam. Christ.  See  I Corinthians 15:21 I Corinthians 15:22 Romans 5:1-21 .

title: I Corinthians 15:50
text: Flesh and blood cannot inherit , etc. Perishable combinations of matter are on a lower plane than the spiritual principle of life; they cannot 'inherit' the kingdom of God.  The apostle implies that only a spiritual body, free from the limitations of the earthly body, can enter into and abide forever in the spiritual kingdom.  See  John 3:6 II Corinthians 5:1 II Corinthians 5:4 .

title: I Corinthians 15:51
text:
:54
 
 Behold. Calling attention to something of great importance.
 

 
 A mystery. Something that can be known only by revelation, and even then cannot be fully explained to the human mind, nor understood by it in its present state.  See  John 16:12 II Corinthians 12:4 .
 

 
 We all. This does not necessarily imply that Paul himself expected to be alive at the moment of the change mentioned.  He speaks in the first person, as one of the Christian host, including all believers living or yet to live.  So 'we' in  I Corinthians 15:52 .
 

 
 Changed, in a moment. A suggestion of what such a change may be appears in accounts of the transfigured before them.  See  Matthew 17:2 Mark 9:2 Luke 9:29 .

title: I Corinthians 15:54
text:
, 55
 
 But when this corruptible, etc. The two texts, 'Death is swallowed up,' etc. and 'O death, where is thy victory,' form together what has been well called 'a song of triumph.'

title: I Corinthians 15:58
text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, etc. After the thanksgiving in  I Corinthians 15:57 , an exhortation to unshaken firmness and earnest work naturally follows, since the sufferings and the labor shall not be vain in the sure triumph of the resurrection.

title: I Corinthians 16:1
text: The collection for the saints. Alluding to the contributions for the poor Christians of Jerusalem during a period of hardships, while the Gentile churches were, in general, wealthy by comparison.  Paul had especially arranged with the other apostles for such charity ( Galatians 2:10 ).  See  Acts 24:17 Romans 15:25 Romans 15:26 II Corinthians 8:1-24 II Corinthians 9:1-15 .

title: I Corinthians 16:2
text:
Upon the first day of the week. That this was then observed as the day of Christian worship is indicated in  Acts 20:7 Revelation of John 1:10 
 

 
 Lay by him in store. That is, at home, put into a special fund, available when needed.
 

 
 That no collections be made when I come. That it be not necessary then to take up a special collection on the spur of the moment.  This verse suggests the propriety of weekly offerings, though it was written for a special occasion and purpose.

title: I Corinthians 16:3
text:
, 4
 
 And when I arrive, etc. An arrangement for the transmission of funds by accredited and responsible agents.  Paul studied businesslike methods in handling benevolent funds, that all might be 'honorable not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.' ( II Corinthians 8:19-21 ).

title: I Corinthians 16:5
text: For I pass through Macedonia. Apparently a change from a previous plan, for which reason some charged the apostle with fickleness ( II Corinthians 1:17 II Corinthians 1:23 ).

title: I Corinthians 16:6
text: It may be that I shall abide, or even winter. This he afterwards found himself able to do ( Acts 20:2 Acts 20:3 ).

title: I Corinthians 16:7
text: I do not wish to see you now by the way. That is, in a hasty visit, and before this epistle should have done its work. See  II Corinthians 1:23 II Corinthians 2:4 .

title: I Corinthians 16:8
text:
I will tarry at Ephesus. Where he then was, indicating that this epistle was written from Ephesus.
 

 
 Pentecost. The great Jewish festival occurring in June, fifty days after the Passover.  See  Acts 2:1 .

title: I Corinthians 16:10
text: Timothy.  See  Acts 16:1-3 .  Timothy seems, from many references, to have been of a shy and timid nature.  Hence the special commendation and charge here given.  See  II Timothy 1:4-8 .

title: I Corinthians 16:12
text: Apollos. See note on 1Co 1.12.  Apollos seems purposely to have remained away at this time, that his presence might not tend to maintain a party among his admirers.

title: I Corinthians 16:15
text:
, 17
 
 Stephanas. See  I Corinthians 1:16 .  Stephanas had come to visit Paul at Ephesus ( I Corinthians 16:17 ), his family apparently remaining at Corinth.

title: I Corinthians 16:21
text: The salutation of me, Paul, etc The previous part of the epistle had been written, as usual, by an amanuensis from dictation; this and the following verses Paul wrote with his own hand, thus authenticating the whole.

title: I Corinthians 16:22
text: Anathema, etc. This word denotes something devoted to destruction.  It is not to be understood here in the spirit of bitterness often attached to the word. See note on  I Corinthians 12:3  also  Romans 9:3 , where 'anathema from Christ' evidently means an outcast from his mercy and the blessings of his gospel.

title: I Corinthians 16:23
text:
, 24
 
 The grace, etc. This closing message of love and grace shows the spirit in which  I Corinthians 16:22 , is written.

title: II Corinthians 1:1
text:
And Timothy. At the time of the writing of this epistle Timothy was with Paul in Macedonia.  See  II Corinthians 9:2 .
 

 
 The whole of Achaia. Achaia occupied the southern part of the peninsula of Greece; Macedonia the northern part.

title: II Corinthians 1:4
text: Who comforteth us.  The comfort for which Paul praises God seems to have resulted from the good reports brought from Corinth by Titus.  See  II Corinthians 7:6 II Corinthians 7:7 II Corinthians 7:13 .

title: II Corinthians 1:5
text: As the sufferings of Christ abound unto us. Much of the suffering of the Man of Sorrows was due to the refusal of the world to accept his message.  See  Luke 13:34 .  Paul suffered from the same baffled yearning.  See  II Corinthians 1:6 II Corinthians 1:7 .

title: II Corinthians 1:8
text: Our affliction which befell us in Asia.  This affliction is believed to have been a severe illness at Ephesus.

title: II Corinthians 1:11
text: The gift bestowed upon us by means of many. The gift was Paul's health restored through the prayers of many.  Paul was a firm believer in the efficacy of united prayers.  See  Romans 15:30 Philippians 1:19 Philemon 1:22 .

title: II Corinthians 1:12
text: Not in fleshy wisdom. 'The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God'. ( I Corinthians 3:19 )

title: II Corinthians 1:14
text: The day of our Lord Jesus.  The day when Christ shall reign supreme.  See  I Corinthians 1:8 Philippians 1:6 Philippians 1:10 Philippians 2:16 .

title: II Corinthians 1:15
text: To come first unto you.  Paul had planned to visit the Corinthians on his way to Macedonia, and again as he returned.  His defense against fickleness indicates that this charge had been brought against him.  See note  II Corinthians 1:23 .

title: II Corinthians 1:17
text: According to the flesh... the yea yea and the nay nay.  This is a denial that he would say one thing meaning another.

title: II Corinthians 1:22
text: @ The earnest of the Spirit.  Earnest money was a small sum paid to bind a bargain.  The earnest of the Spirit is a pledge of complete salvation.

title: II Corinthians 1:23
text: To spare you I forbare to come unto Corinth. The innference must be that had Paul gone to Corinth at the time expected it would have been with a rod of correction.  See  I Corinthians 4:21 ; also  II Corinthians 2:1-3 .

title: II Corinthians 1:24
text: Lordship over your faith. This is a declaration of entire freedom to every man, in the working out of his own salvation ( Philippians 2:12 ).  See  II Corinthians 4:5 I Peter 5:3 .

title: II Corinthians 2:1
text:
9
 
 Obedient in all things. This obedience was not toward Paul, but 'obedience to Christ' ( II Corinthians 10:5 II Corinthians 10:6 ).  See also  II Corinthians 1:24 , and note thereon.

title: II Corinthians 2:6
text: Inflicted by the many. Paul's letter had wrought its intended result, and the church had purged itself.  See  I Corinthians 5:1-13 .  Paul now counsels forgiveness ( II Corinthians 2:7 ).

title: II Corinthians 2:11
text: That no advantage may be gained over us by Satan. Paul feared that in the zeal of their condemnation of the sin, Satan would craftily trick them into hatred of the erring brother, to whom he beseeches them to confirm their love ( II Corinthians 2:8 ), by forgiveness and comfort ( II Corinthians 2:7 ).

title: II Corinthians 2:13
text: Because I found not Titus. Titus had been the bearer of the letter mentioned in  II Corinthians 2:4 , and Paul's anxiety as to the outcome was so intense that he could not remain and work in Troas, where indeed he found a welcome ( II Corinthians 2:12 ).  He hastened onward to meet Titus, which he did in Macedonia ( II Corinthians 7:5 II Corinthians 7:6 ).

title: II Corinthians 2:15
text: A sweet savor.  The expression is symbolical, borrowed from the Jewish ceremony of burnt-offerings.  See  Genesis 8:21 Exodus 29:18 .

title: II Corinthians 2:16
text: A savor from death unto death. The revelation of Christ in the gospel came to those dead in trespasses and sins.  Those who accepted it, passed from death into life ( John 5:24 ).  To those who rejected it, it became the deeper condemnation.  See  John 9:39-41 .

title: II Corinthians 2:17
text: The many. Those Jewish teachers who were insisting that the Gentile converts must be circumcised - made into Jews - before they could be received into the church.

title: II Corinthians 3:3
text: Tables of stone. The Mosaic law- the law of outward behavior- was written upon tables of stone ( Exodus 24:12 ). The epistle written by Paul upon the hearts of the Corinthians was the law of love - of righteousness for its own sake, through the grace of Christ.  See  Ephesians 2:8 Acts 15:11 .

title: II Corinthians 3:7
text:
The ministration of death. The Mosaic law was a law of discipline, enforced by penalties, and upheld by the fear of the visitation of death upon the evil-doer through the wrath of God.  See  Joshua 7:26 .
 

 
 For the glory of his face. When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, with the tables of the law, 'the skin of his face shone.' See  Exodus 34:29-35 .

title: II Corinthians 3:9
text: The ministration of condemnation. See note on  II Corinthians 3:7 .  Through Adam came the judgment unto condemnation (Ro 5.16-18); but, 'there is therefore now no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus' ( Romans 8:1 ).

title: II Corinthians 3:13
text: Who put a veil upon his face.  See  Exodus 34:33 Exodus 34:35 .

title: II Corinthians 3:14
text: The same veil remaineth.  The language is figurative: the veil which remained was the belief of the hardened Jewish heart in the sacredness of the old covenant (of the law), which prevented the realization that it had passed away under the new covenant in Christ.

title: II Corinthians 3:15
text: A veil lieth upon their heart. Many scholars see in this passage a reference to the Jewish custom of covering the head with a four-cornered veil called the tallith, when they were in the synagogue.  The tallith did not cover the eyes but hung down over the breast.

title: II Corinthians 3:17
text: Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. The bondage under the law of the 'thou shalt' and the 'thou shalt not' disappears in the presence of the Spirit of adoption ( Galatians 4:7 ) through which we become 'imitators of God as beloved children' ( Ephesians 5:1 ), walking in love. See  Romans 8:2 .

title: II Corinthians 4:1
text: Even as we obtained mercy. Paul kept continually in mind the fact that he had been a persecutor of the Christians.  His salvation was the greater mercy.  See  I Timothy 1:13 .

title: II Corinthians 4:3
text: It is veiled in them that perish.  See notes  II Corinthians 2:16 II Corinthians 3:14 ; also  I Corinthians 1:18 .

title: II Corinthians 4:7
text: In earthern vessels. The idea conveyed is that the fragile nature of the human means through which the gospel is spread only exhibits the greater power in the gospel itself which borrows nothing from its ministers.  On the contrary, the vessel is exalted by the treasure it contains.  See  I Corinthians 2:3-5 .

title: II Corinthians 4:10
text:
The dying of Jesus. To Paul the dying of Jesus symbolized the death of the desires of the flesh toward sin.  As he writes to the Romans: - 'Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him that the body of sin might be done away with.'  See  Romans 6:5-7 Romans 8:6 Romans 8:10 Romans 8:13 .
 

 
 That the life also of Jesus. The word life here is to be construed spiritually;- the inward regeneration as manifest in the outward life in the flesh.  'It is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me' ( Galatians 2:20 ).  See  Romans 8:11 .

title: II Corinthians 4:12
text: So then death worketh in us, but life in you. The death as to the flesh, manifest in the apostle, became life in those who saw and believed.  See  Romans 6:4 .

title: II Corinthians 4:16
text: Though our outward man is decaying. Paul is speaking of the infirmities of disease and old age; the inward man, having been begotten again of incorruptible seed is continually renewed through growth in grace.  See  Ephesians 4:23 Ephesians 4:24 I Peter 1:23 .

title: II Corinthians 4:18
text: The things which are seen are temporal. The spiritual things are the real things.  'The world passeth away and the lust (desires) thereof' ( I John 2:17 ).  The whole structure of modern civilization, with all its achievements and so-called riches and possessions for which men strive, shall God 'bring to nought' ( I Corinthians 6:13 ). See  I Corinthians 7:31 ; also  Matthew 6:20 Galatians 5:22 .

title: II Corinthians 5:1
text: Tabernacle. The tabernacle was a temporary tent.  See  Exodus 26:1 .  With this Paul contrasts the permanent 'habitation which is from heaven' ( II Corinthians 5:2 ), for which he longs.

title: II Corinthians 5:4
text:
Being burdened. The burden of human life is the continual warfare of the desires of the flesh against the spirit ( Romans 7:15-24 ).
 

 
 Not for that we would be unclothed. Paul's desire was not to escape the conflicts with the mortal body by death, but that the mortal should 'put on immortality' ( I Corinthians 15:53 ).

title: II Corinthians 5:5
text: The earnest of the Spirit. The intense desire unto spiritual things is an earnest of the immortal life.  See note  II Corinthians 1:22 .

title: II Corinthians 5:6
text:
At home in the body. The phrase signifies satisfaction with the human life - the life of the world, as compared with the ardent desire to 'lay hold on the life which is life indeed' ( I Timothy 6:19 ).  See  Philippians 3:12 Philippians 3:14 Revelation of John 3:20 .
 

 
 Absent from the Lord. Christ is indeed with us here and always; but, in the clearer vision of the life to come, our realization of his presence will make this present existence to have been absence by comparison.

title: II Corinthians 5:10
text: The judgment-seat of Christ. The 'fulness of Christ' is the measure to which stature we must all attain ( Ephesians 4:13 ); and God 'will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he hath ordained' ( Acts 17:31 ).  See  John 3:19 John 9:39 .

title: II Corinthians 5:11
text:
The fear of the Lord. This is the fear inspired by love, lest we should fail of reaching the stature of the fulness of Christ.  See preceding note.
 

 
 Made manifest also in your consciences. Paul is confident as to his manifestation unto God, who regards not the outward appearance, but 'looketh on the heart' ( I Samuel 16:7 ); he hopes that his manifestation of the Christ is recognized by the Corinthians.

title: II Corinthians 5:14
text: Therefore all died. The death all died with Christ was death as to sin under the law.  As Paul says ( Romans 7:4 ): - 'Wherefore, my brethren, ye also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ.' And again: - 'It is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me' ( Galatians 2:20 ).  See also  Romans 6:6-11 Galatians 2:19 .

title: II Corinthians 5:18
text: Who reconciled us to himself through Christ. This reconciliation to God is explained by Paul ( Romans 5:10 ) as 'through the death of his Son' much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.' See following note.

title: II Corinthians 5:21
text: Him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf.  Jesus came 'in the likeness of sinful flesh' ( Romans 8:3 ) and was 'in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin' ( Hebrews 4:15 ).

title: II Corinthians 6:1
text:
Working together with him. Paul says in  I Corinthians 1:21 ;- 'It was God's good pleasure through the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe, 'and in this work he recognized the help of the Lord. See  Mark 16:20 I Corinthians 3:9 .
 

 
 Grace of God. What the grace of God is meant to effect is clearly set forth in Titus 2.11, 12:- 'For the grace of God hath appeared bringing salvation to all men, instructing us, to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly and righteously and godly in this present world.'

title: II Corinthians 6:4
text: In everything commending ourselves. Paul here, in the verses following, recites his record of persecutions endured and of deeds performed, as well the results of his preaching, as a truer commendation than if he had borne letters from the heads of the Judaic Christians at Rome.  It was as if he had quoted the worlds of Jesus:- 'By their fruits ye shall know them' ( Matthew 7:16-20 ).

title: II Corinthians 6:11
text: Our moth is open... our heart is enlarged. As Paul's heart goes out toward the Corinthians in a larger flood of affection, he does not weigh his words, but writes boldly, with the power of inspiration. See  II Corinthians 7:4 .

title: II Corinthians 6:12
text: Ye are not straitened in us. If the Corinthians were narrow or cramped in their reception of the gospel, it was not because Paul's ministry had been lacking in fulness.

title: II Corinthians 6:14
text: Be not unequally yoked with unbelievers. There can be no real partnership when the spiritual natures are diverse. Jesus voiced the same warning in his utterance: 'Ye cannot serve God and mammon' ( Matthew 6:24 ).  Paul follows up his argument ( II Corinthians 6:16 ) with the exhortation:- 'Come ye out from among them and be ye separate' ( II Corinthians 6:17 ).  See  Revelation of John 18:4 ; also  I Corinthians 5:9 I Corinthians 5:11 .

title: II Corinthians 6:15
text: Belial. The word in the Hebrew signifies 'worthlessness.' It is here used as a name for Satan.

title: II Corinthians 7:2
text: Open your hearts to us. The Corinthians had been listening to charges that Paul was not preaching the true gospel, and that he was preaching for gain.  He asks a fair hearing.  See  II Corinthians 11:4 II Corinthians 11:7-9 II Corinthians 12:14 II Corinthians 12:17 II Corinthians 12:18 .

title: II Corinthians 7:5
text: When we were come into Macedonia.  See note  II Corinthians 2:13 ; also  Romans 15:26 .

title: II Corinthians 7:12
text: Your earnest care for us. The real intent of Paul's letter of rebuke was to recall the Corinthians to loyalty to his teachings.  See  I Corinthians 5:1-7 .

title: II Corinthians 7:15
text: Fear and trembling. Anxiety that he should find them free of need for censure.

title: II Corinthians 8:2
text: The riches of their liberality. The Gentile churches of Macedonia, though themselves in deep poverty, had sent a contribution to the poor Jewish Christians at Jerusalem.  See  Romans 15:26 .  The Macedonian churches mentioned in the New Testament are those of Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea.

title: II Corinthians 8:6
text: This grace also. It would appear that the Corinthians were lacking in ordinary generosity.  When Paul was preaching among them he was supported by funds contributed by other churches, the church at Philippi being his dependence.  See  Philippians 4:15 . The churches in Macedonia had given of their own accord ( II Corinthians 8:3 ): the Corinthians had to be asked for their contribution by Titus.

title: II Corinthians 8:18
text: The brother whose praise... is spread through all the churches. No clue is given as to the identity of this brother.  Some commentators surmise that he was Luke; others, Tychicus, so often Paul's faithful messenger.  See  Acts 20:4 ; also note following.

title: II Corinthians 8:22
text: Our brother. Also unknown. The two who accompanied Titus to gather the collection were probably delegated by the contributing churches at Paul's request ( II Corinthians 8:20 ).  One may have been Epaphroditus, the messenger of the church at Philippi to Paul at Rome.  See  Philippians 2:25 .

title: II Corinthians 8:24
text: Our glorying on your behalf. See  II Corinthians 7:14 II Corinthians 9:2 .  See note  II Corinthians 9:4 .

title: II Corinthians 9:2
text: Achaia hath been prepared for a year past. Corinth was the centre of Achaian activity, and the church there had been the first to propose aiding the poor among the Jewish brethren at Jerusalem and had actually made a beginning a year previously.  See  II Corinthians 8:10 .

title: II Corinthians 9:7
text: Not grudgingly. The grudging gift is tainted with covetousness.  Only that part of a gift which is freely given is worthy to be called bounty (blessing).  Paul urges the bountiful giving while warning against the hypocrisy of the grudging gift.  See  Philippians 4:17 .

title: II Corinthians 9:13
text: Through the proving of you by this ministration. The contributions of the Gentiles to the Jews were evidence of their unity with them in brotherly love, as one church.  The establishing of this spirit of unity in Christ was greatly desired by Paul.  See  I Corinthians 10:17 I Corinthians 12:13 Ephesians 4:5 Colossians 3:11 .

title: II Corinthians 9:14
text: The exceeding grace of God in you. See  I Corinthians 1:4 I Corinthians 1:5 .

title: II Corinthians 10:1
text: Lowly among you. Paul was slow to assume a lordship over the Corinthians ( II Corinthians 1:24 ) even to the extent of administering a rebuke in person.  See  II Corinthians 2:1-3 .

title: II Corinthians 10:2
text: Bold against some. Paul had personal enemies in the church at Corinth who found fault with his conduct ( II Corinthians 1:17 ) and with his teachings.  Against these he would be bold.  See also  II Corinthians 10:12 .

title: II Corinthians 10:5
text:
Exalted against the knowledge of God. The chief scourge of the early Christian church was the body of false teachers who sprang up and deceived many by their worldly interpretations of the gospel.  See  Matthew 24:24 I Timothy 1:6 I Timothy 1:7 II Peter 2:1 .
 

 
 Into captivity to the obedience of Christ. The false teachers seized upon Christianity as an excuse to escape obedience as to the law, and claimed freedom from sin through the sacrifice of Christ, while still remaining in unrighteousness.

title: II Corinthians 10:7
text: Ye look at the things that are before your face.   According to outward appearance.

title: II Corinthians 10:8
text: Our authority. Paul's mission to the Gentiles rested upon a special divine appointment.  See  Acts 9:15 .

title: II Corinthians 10:10
text: His bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account. Paul was not masterful in demeanor, but lowly ( II Corinthians 10:1 ); and though noted for his eloquence  ( Acts 14:12 ), he was persuasive, not dominating ( II Corinthians 1:24 ).

title: II Corinthians 10:12
text: Comparing themselves with themselves. The value of a comparison depends upon the standard.  Paul measures himself by the magnitude of the work entrusted to him.

title: II Corinthians 10:13
text: To reach even unto you. The gospel was given primarily to the Jews only.  Through the commissioning of Paul it was extended even unto the Gentiles; that is, to the whole world.

title: II Corinthians 10:15
text: Not glorying... in other men's labors.  The inference here is that Paul's opponents had seized upon the organized church at Corinth, the fruit of Paul's labors, as a ready made field for their 'imaginations' ( II Corinthians 10:5 ). Paul suggests that there is abundant territory still untouched in 'the parts beyond you.' See  II Corinthians 10:16 .

title: II Corinthians 11:1
text: A little foolishness.  In stooping to meet the accusations as to his conduct 'according to the flesh' Paul places the quibble in its proper light as foolishness.  Paul, while building up the church at Corinth, had supported himself with the aid of other churches ( II Corinthians 11:8 ).  His enemies had craftily charged that he had not asked contributions for his support because he knew that the gospel he preached was worthless.

title: II Corinthians 11:5
text: Not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles. When Paul had visited Jerusalem to confer with the apostles who had been with Jesus they could add nothing to his knowledge of the gospel.  See  Acts 15:2 Galatians 2:6 .

title: II Corinthians 11:6
text: In every way have we made this manifest. At the gathering of the apostles and elders at Jerusalem to hear Paul, he and Barnabas recounted the 'signs and wonders' which had attended their ministry.  See  Acts 15:12 John 4:48 .

title: II Corinthians 11:9
text: And was in want. There is a sting of reproach in  this simple statement of fact.  The Corinthians had not taken thought as to Paul's daily necessities while he labored among them.  His wants were relieved by others; and yet they hearkened to criticism of him for bearing in silence their own shortcomings.  See  I Corinthians 9:11 I Corinthians 9:12 .

title: II Corinthians 11:13
text: For such men are false apostles. The test of true fellowship in Christ, as laid down by the apostles, was the love of the brethren.  See  I Peter 1:22 I John 3:14 I John 3:19 .

title: II Corinthians 11:17
text: I speak not after the Lord, but as in foolishness. Paul administers a rebuke, even as he answers the charges against him:- these things were not of the Lord, therefore foolishness.  But even in his conduct as to the foolish things of the flesh he glories that he has been the giver and not a dependent on unwilling bounty.

title: II Corinthians 11:20
text: For ye bear with a man, etc.  After asking that the Corinthians bear with him in his fancy of bringing them the gospel without cost to them ( I Corinthians 9:12 ), even though he suffered want in doing so, he offers as a reason for expecting this favor, a catalogue of the opposite characteristics of his enemy whom they had gladly received and listened to.

title: II Corinthians 11:23
text: As one beside himself. The idea of calling such a man ( II Corinthians 11:20 ) a minister of Christ, even for the purpose of comparison, is devoid of all reason.  And here the parallel breaks down, for Paul's accuser has no record of afflictions and persecutions to match the history of Paul.

title: II Corinthians 11:24
text: Forty stripes save one. The penalty of forty stripes, under the Jewish law, was coupled with an injunction that this number should not be exceeded. Lest a mistake be made in the count it was customary to cease with the thirty-ninth stroke.  See  Deuteronomy 25:3 .  These scourgings are not recorded in The Acts.  One of the beatings with rods was at Philippi ( Acts 16:22 ), and the stoning was at Lystra ( Acts 14:19 ).

title: II Corinthians 11:30
text: I will glory of the things that concern my weakness. Paul's achievements, he knew, were by the power of Christ working in him ( Colossians 1:29 ).  For himself all he could boast of were the sufferings he had endured in the service.

title: II Corinthians 11:33
text: Through a window was I let down in a basket.  See  Acts 9:25 .

title: II Corinthians 12:1
text: I must needs glory. The attitude of the Corinthians toward Paul's accuser forced him to recount to them circumstances which would tend to prove his devotion to the cause of Christ.  But even this he did under protest.

title: II Corinthians 12:2
text: Fourteen years ago. The vision on the road to Damascus ( Acts 9:3 ) had occurred about twenty years before; and it is generally believed that the vision here referred to is that in the Temple, recorded in  Acts 22:17 .

title: II Corinthians 12:4
